etymology: From the Saxon rædels, “a thing to be read, guessed, or counselled,” from rædan, to read or advise; rendering the Hebrew chidah, a knotted or twisted saying — speech folded over on itself so that it must be untied before it will yield.
biblical_def: A riddle is a saying deliberately knotted, propounded that it may be unriddled. Samson sets one at his wedding feast with thirty sheets and thirty change of garments upon the wager: “Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Jdg 14:14), and the Philistines could not expound it in three days — they got the answer only by threatening his wife, which is how the flesh always deals with what it cannot discern. Ezekiel is commanded, “Son of man, put forth a riddle, and speak a parable unto the house of Israel” (Eze 17:2), the eagle and the cedar; and the LORD Himself supplies the interpretation within the same chapter, which is the whole doctrine of the thing. Solomon sets the riddle inside the course of wisdom: the wise man learns “to understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings” (Pro 1:6). The riddle is therefore no game of divine concealment. God reveals Himself truly, though never exhaustively; He wraps some truth that His people may dig for it, and that the scorner may stumble at it. To Moses He spoke “not in dark speeches” (Num 12:8); to the multitude Christ spoke in parables, that seeing they might not see (Mat 13:13). The same knot is a handle to the believing and a wall to the hardened.
webster_summary: An enigma; a proposition put in obscure or ambiguous terms to exercise the wit of him who would find it out.
webster_full: RIDDLE, n. [Sax. rædels, from rædan, to read, to counsel.] An enigma; something proposed for conjecture, or that is to be solved by conjecture.
Anything ambiguous or puzzling; a dark saying which must be interpreted before it is understood.
To riddle, v. To solve; to explain; to unriddle a dark saying.
In Scripture it renders the Hebrew chidah, a knot or twisted speech, used of Samson’s wager (Jdg 14:12) and of Ezekiel’s parable of the eagle (Eze 17:2).
Distinguished from a lie: a riddle conceals truth for a season that it may be sought; a lie destroys it.
scriptures: And Samson said unto them, I will now put forth a riddle unto you: if ye can certainly declare it me within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty sheets and thirty change of garments:
And he said unto them, Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle.
Eze 17:2
Son of man, put forth a riddle, and speak a parable unto the house of Israel;
Pro 1:6
To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings.
corruption_summary: The riddle is turned into a doctrine of Scripture itself — the Bible recast as an esoteric puzzle whose meaning waits upon experts, mystics, or codes, against the perspicuity the Reformation recovered.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome long taught the people that the Book was too dark for them, and the modern academy teaches the same thing in a new dialect: the text is a riddle that only the credentialed may untie. To this the sects add their own key — Bible codes counted out in letters, numerological schemes, date-setting charts, gnostic “hidden gospels,” the fashionable claim that every plain command conceals a mystery the initiated alone can read. All of it inverts the Scripture’s own account of itself. The LORD did not put forth the riddle of the eagle and the cedar and leave Israel guessing; He interpreted it in the same breath (Eze 17:11–21). Ezekiel’s riddle is a rhetorical arrest, not a lock. Where God speaks in figure He also speaks in exposition, and the exposition is in the canon, not in a private key held over the church’s head. The 1689 Confession states the rule plainly: those things necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation are so clearly propounded that not only the learned but the unlearned, in a due use of ordinary means, may attain a sufficient understanding of them.

There is a second and opposite error: treating everything hard as though it were nothing. Peter granted that in Paul’s epistles are “some things hard to be understood” (2Pe 3:16), and the man who denies it will simply flatten the text into his own opinions. Recover both halves. God reveals Himself truly but not exhaustively; the secret things belong unto the LORD, the things revealed unto us and to our children (Deu 29:29). A riddle in Scripture is an invitation to labour with an open Bible, a concordance, and the ordinary means of grace, not an excuse for private revelation or for despair. Samson’s riddle was cracked by treachery; Ezekiel’s was opened by God; and the parables of Christ were expounded to His disciples in the house (Mar 4:34). The pattern holds for us: the Lord who folds a saying is the Lord who unfolds it, and He does it by His Word and by His Spirit, never apart from them.
roots_summary: Saxon rædels, a thing to be read out; Hebrew chidah, a knotted saying to be untied.
roots_lines: Riddle — Saxon rædels, from rædan, to read, to counsel.
Hebrew chidah (Strong’s H2420) — a knot, a dark saying, an enigma.
Samson’s wager at Timnath is the chief narrative instance (Jdg 14:12–18).
Ezekiel’s riddle of the eagle and the cedar is interpreted by God in the same chapter (Eze 17:2, 11–21).
Paired with parable and dark sayings as the wise man’s study (Pro 1:6; Psa 78:2).
usage: A riddle in Scripture is truth folded, not truth withheld — and God supplies the unfolding.
Ezekiel’s riddle came with its own interpretation; no secret key was left in another man’s hand.
The hard places drive us to labour, not to a guru; the necessary things are plain to the unlearned.

etymology: A compound of by (aside, secondary) and word: a saying passed about at the side of serious speech — a taunt-name, a proverb of contempt. It renders the Hebrew millah and mashal when the proverb has turned to mockery.
biblical_def: A byword is a name that has become a taunt — a people or a person made into the world’s proverb of scorn. It stands in Scripture first as a covenant curse. Moses warned Israel at the edge of the land: “thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations whither the LORD shall lead thee” (Deu 28:37). The LORD repeats it to Solomon at the dedication of the very house he had built: if Israel turn from His commandments, “Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people” (1Ki 9:7). This is the sharpest edge of the curse, sharper than famine or sword, because it is the loss of witness. A nation raised to show the nations the glory of the true God becomes instead the joke of the nations, and the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through them (Rom 2:24). But the same word is laid upon a righteous man who has done nothing to earn it: “He hath made me also a byword of the people” (Job 17:6), and again, “now am I their song, yea, I am their byword” (Job 30:9). Asaph’s sons cry it corporately: “Thou makest us a byword among the heathen” (Psa 44:14). Here the reproach is not punishment but proving, and it points forward — for He who was despised and rejected of men bore in full what Job bore in part.
webster_summary: A common saying; a proverb; and hence a name of reproach, a person or people made the object of a scornful proverb.
webster_full: BYWORD, n. [by and word.] A common saying; a proverb; a saying that has a general currency.
A term of reproach; an object of contempt, whose very name has become a proverb of scorn.
“Thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword” (Deu 28:37) — the covenant curse of lost witness.
Applied to the righteous under affliction: “I am their byword” (Job 30:9).
Distinguished from a mere word: a byword is speech that has hardened into a public judgment upon a name.
scriptures: And thou shalt become an astonishment, a proverb, and a byword, among all nations whither the LORD shall lead thee.

Then will I cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have hallowed for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people:
Job 17:6
He hath made me also a byword of the people; and aforetime I was as a tabret.
Thou makest us a byword among the heathen, a shaking of the head among the people.
corruption_summary: Respectability is made the measure of faithfulness: churches govern doctrine and preaching by what will keep them from becoming a byword, forgetting that Christ promised His people exactly that reproach.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is not a redefinition of the word but a reversal of its verdict. A congregation reads Deu 28:37, sees that becoming a byword is a curse, and concludes that avoiding the world’s scorn is therefore a mark of blessing. So the hard doctrines are muted — hell, sexual purity, the exclusivity of Christ, the creational order of headship — lest the church become a proverb among the nations. But Scripture draws the line elsewhere. Israel became a byword for apostasy: the reproach came upon a people whose sin had made the name of God contemptible. Job became a byword for righteousness, and God vindicated him and rebuked his accusers. The reproach of Christ is a treasure (Heb 11:26); the reproach of a sinning church is a scandal. To flee all reproach indiscriminately is to flee the cross, for the Lord said plainly that men shall revile you and say all manner of evil against you falsely, for His sake, and called that blessedness.

The postmodern handling of the word runs the other direction: reproach is converted into proof, and every accusation of scorn is treated as evidence of righteousness, so that no rebuke can ever land. Both errors are cured by asking one question — why is the name a byword? Recover Job’s posture. He does not deny the reproach, he does not glory in it, and he does not silence his conscience with it; he carries it to God and waits for a Redeemer who lives and shall stand at the latter day upon the earth (Job 19:25). That is the shape of the thing for the church. Where we are a byword because of sin, repent and remove the occasion. Where we are a byword because of Christ, endure it, bless them that curse, and remember that our Head was numbered with the transgressors and made a shaking of the head among the people before us.
roots_summary: By + word: a saying passed around at the side, and thence a name handed over to public contempt.
roots_lines: Byword — Saxon bi (near, aside) + word: speech in common circulation.
Renders Hebrew millah (a word, a taunt-saying) and stands beside mashal, a proverb.
Covenant-curse language of Deuteronomy 28, repeated to Solomon at the temple (1Ki 9:7).
Paired with astonishment and a shaking of the head (Deu 28:37; Psa 44:14).
Job’s use turns it: the righteous sufferer bears the taunt he did not earn (Job 17:6; 30:9).
usage: Israel a byword is the curse of lost witness — the nations mocking the God whose name she bore.
Job a byword is the reproach of the righteous, and it prefigures the Man of sorrows.
Ask why the name is scorned before you either flee the scorn or boast in it.

etymology: From the Saxon tael, kin to tell and to German Zahl, number. The older and primary sense is a reckoning or tally; the secondary sense is a thing told. Both senses stand in the Authorized Version, and the reader who knows only the second will misread the first.
biblical_def: Tale in the Authorized Version carries two senses, and they must not be confused. The older sense is a tally, a counted number. Pharaoh’s taskmasters demand, “Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks” (Exo 5:18) — not a story about bricks but the daily quota, the count unabated though the straw is gone. So too David “brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full tale to the king” (1Sa 18:27): a full reckoning, numbered out. The second sense is the thing narrated. Moses prays, “we spend our years as a tale that is told” (Psa 90:9) — a life reeled off and finished, the whole of it briefer than the telling. And Luke records the apostolic company’s first response to the resurrection: the women’s report of the empty tomb “seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not” (Luk 24:11). That verse is the honest confession of the church’s own founders: the men who would die for the risen Christ first dismissed the news as nonsense, and were persuaded only by the Lord Himself, who upbraided them for their unbelief and hardness of heart. The witnesses were not credulous. They were the hardest to convince of all.
webster_summary: First, a number reckoned or told over — a tally or quota; second, a narrative or story, and in a bad sense an idle report.
webster_full: TALE, n. [Sax. tael, number; allied to tell, to count.] Number reckoned; a reckoning; as, the tale of bricks (Exo 5:18).
“In their conquests they took no account of the number slain, but only of the tale of the prisoners.” Hence to tell money is to count it.
A narrative or relation; a story, true or fictitious, told or written.
An idle or malicious report; hence a talebearer, one who carries such reports about.
The double sense is native to the word: to tell is both to count and to recount.
scriptures: Exo 5:18
Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you, yet shall ye deliver the tale of bricks.

Wherefore David arose and went, he and his men, and slew of the Philistines two hundred men; and David brought their foreskins, and they gave them in full tale to the king, that he might be the king's son in law. And Saul gave him Michal his daughter to wife.
Psa 90:9
For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.
And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not.
corruption_summary: Historical criticism reclassifies the biblical narratives as tales — “mythological elements” and “legendary material” in the canon — and so grants the apostles’ first unbelief the last word.
corruption_paragraphs: The academic corruption is precise and must be named. Since the nineteenth century the dominant guild has handled Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Jonah, and the resurrection narratives under the headings of “mythological elements” and “legendary material” — the flood a borrowed Mesopotamian tale, the exodus a national epic, the empty tomb a late accretion of the believing community. Popular religion follows at a distance: the Bible becomes a book of stories with morals attached, useful for children, not a record of what God actually did in time and space. This is Luk 24:11 made permanent. The disciples’ first verdict — idle tales — is precisely the verdict the guild renders, only dressed in method. But Luke did not record that verdict to endorse it; he recorded it to destroy it, and the Lord Himself answered it by eating broiled fish and a honeycomb before them and showing them His hands and His feet. Peter puts it beyond dispute: “we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16).

Recover the sober double sense of the word, for both edges cut. The tally sense preaches: Pharaoh demands the full count of bricks and takes away the straw, which is the exact temper of every taskmaster since — the law of sin exacting the quota it will not supply the means to meet. Only Christ gives rest to men crushed under such a reckoning. The narrative sense preaches too, but in Moses’ direction: our years are spent as a tale that is told, begun and ended in a breath, and the man who has not numbered his days has not begun to be wise. Set these against the modern reduction. Scripture is not a tale; it is testimony, sworn, dated, and public, given by men who first refused to believe it and afterward were slain rather than deny it. Faith rests on the report of God, and the report of God is fact before it is ever comfort.
roots_summary: Saxon tael, number — kin to tell: to count and to recount are one word in the older English.
roots_lines: Tale — Saxon tael, number, reckoning; cognate with German Zahl and English tell.
Sense 1 (older, primary in the AV): a tally or quota — “the tale of bricks” (Exo 5:18); “in full tale” (1Sa 18:27).
Sense 2: a thing told — “a tale that is told” (Psa 90:9).
Sense 2 in the pejorative: idle tales, Greek lēros, nonsense or delirium (Luk 24:11).
A genuine false friend: modern readers hear “story” where the AV often means “count.”
usage: The tale of bricks is a quota, not a story — Pharaoh demanded the count and withheld the straw.
“A tale that is told” measures the brevity of life, not the truth of a narrative.
The apostles first called the resurrection an idle tale; their later blood is the answer to that verdict.

etymology: From the Latin similitudo, likeness, from similis, like. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew temunah (a visible form or shape) and demuth (likeness), and the Greek homoiōma and homoiōsis.
biblical_def: A similitude is a likeness — either a visible form seen, or a comparison spoken. Both senses bear great doctrinal weight. Of Moses the LORD said, “With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold” (Num 12:8): a nearness of communion granted to no other prophet, yet still not the naked essence, for no man hath seen God at any time. Over against that singular grant stands the sharpest word in the chapter of the second commandment. At Horeb, “ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice” (Deu 4:12), and therefore, “Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb” (Deu 4:15). The argument is exact and binding: God gave Israel a voice and withheld a shape, so that they should make no shape. Israel broke it at Sinai, and the Psalmist writes the epitaph: “Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass” (Psa 106:20). The spoken sense follows the same rule — God taught by similitudes through the prophets (Hos 12:10), by comparison and figure, which is likeness in words rather than likeness in wood and stone.
webster_summary: Likeness; resemblance; a visible form or shape; also a comparison, parable, or figure by which one thing is likened to another.
webster_full: SIMILITUDE, n. [L. similitudo, from similis, like.] Likeness; resemblance; likeness in nature, qualities or appearance.
A visible form or shape; that which is seen of a thing — “ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15).
Comparison; simile; the act of likening one thing to another for instruction.
“I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” (Hos 12:10).
Of man: made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9), and therefore not to be cursed.
scriptures: Num 12:8
With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches; and the similitude of the LORD shall he behold: wherefore then were ye not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?
Deu 4:12
And the LORD spake unto you out of the midst of the fire: ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice.
Deu 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass.
corruption_summary: The second commandment’s ground — no similitude was seen, therefore none may be made — is set aside wherever images of God and of Christ are venerated, printed, filmed, and hung for devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome divided the Decalogue so that the prohibition of images is folded into the first commandment and effectively lost, and the Second Council of Nicaea (787) licensed the veneration of images with a distinction between latria and dulia that Deu 4:15 never grants. The Eastern churches went further and made the icon a channel of devotion. But Moses’ argument is not about the crudeness of the image; it is about the mode of revelation. God came in fire and gave a voice and withheld a shape, on purpose, that His people might worship by hearing and not by seeing. Israel’s first great apostasy was not a denial of the LORD but an image of Him — a calf, hailed as the god that brought them up out of Egypt — and the Psalmist calls that exchange the loss of their glory (Psa 106:20). The Reformed churches recovered the point: the regulative principle of worship follows straight out of Deu 4, and the 1689 Confession forbids the worship of God by images or any other way not prescribed in Holy Scripture.

The modern form is softer and nearly universal. Few Protestants bow to a statue, but the pictured Christ hangs in nurseries, fills flannelgraphs, and walks through films with an actor’s face; and the image, not the text, becomes the mental furniture of the congregation’s piety. It will not do to answer that Christ has a true human nature and may therefore be pictured, for His Person is not divisible: what is depicted is either less than He is or a lie about Him. The Puritans pressed exactly this, and their conclusion deserves a hearing rather than a shrug. Recover the ordinance God actually gave. Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Rom 10:17); the preached Word, the read Word, and the two visible signs Christ Himself instituted are the appointed helps. And note the one similitude Scripture does command us to honour: man himself, made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9), whom we are forbidden to curse.
roots_summary: Latin similitudo, likeness; Hebrew temunah, a visible form — the very thing Israel was not shown.
roots_lines: Similitude — Latin similitudo, from similis, like.
Hebrew temunah (H8544), a visible form or shape (Deu 4:12, 15; Num 12:8).
Hebrew demuth (H1823), likeness — the word of Gen 1:26.
Greek homoiōma / homoiōsis, likeness (Rom 5:14; Jas 3:9).
Second sense: a spoken comparison or figure, the prophets’ teaching method (Hos 12:10).
usage: Deu 4:12–15 is the ground of the second commandment: a voice was given, a shape withheld.
Moses beheld the similitude of the LORD by singular grace; it was never a warrant for images.
Psa 106:20 names image-making an exchange of glory, not a devotional aid.

etymology: From the Latin interpres, a broker or go-between, hence one who explains — inter, between, with a root sense of trading or bearing across. In the AV it renders the Hebrew luts / melits (a spokesman, an intermediary) and the Greek diermeneutēs.
biblical_def: An interpreter is one who carries a meaning across — from a tongue not understood, from a dream, from God to men. Scripture’s governing statement on the office is Joseph’s in the prison house. The butler and baker say they have dreamed and there is no interpreter of the dream, and Joseph answers, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (Gen 40:8). He does not deny that he will interpret; he denies that the interpretation is his. Pharaoh later summons him on report that he can understand a dream to interpret it (Gen 41:15), and Joseph answers the king in the same terms: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Daniel says the same before Nebuchadnezzar. Elihu speaks of a rarer office still — “a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness” (Job 33:23) — a mediating voice that declares to a dying man what God is doing with him, which the New Testament fulfils in the one Mediator. And Paul lays the rule upon the assembly: “if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church” (1Co 14:28). The gift of a tongue without interpretation is not permitted to occupy the congregation. Meaning belongs to God; the church is to be edified, not impressed.
webster_summary: One who explains or expounds; one who translates from a tongue not understood; a go-between who carries a meaning across.
webster_full: INTERPRETER, n. [L. interpres, a broker, an agent between parties.] One that explains or expounds; an expositor.
One that translates from one language to another for the understanding of the hearers.
One who declares the mind of God to men — “an interpreter, one among a thousand” (Job 33:23).
In the church, the one without whom a tongue must be kept silent (1Co 14:28).
Joseph and Daniel are the great scriptural instances, and both refer the interpretation to God (Gen 40:8; Dan 2:28).
scriptures: Gen 40:8
And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.
And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, that thou canst understand a dream to interpret it.
If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness:
But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God.
corruption_summary: Postmodern hermeneutics relocates meaning from the text to the reader — “the text means what it means to me” — making every man his own interpreter and no man accountable to God’s own sense.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning error of the age is reader-response interpretation: the claim that a text has no fixed sense of its own, that meaning is produced by the reader’s community and situation, and that to speak of what a passage means apart from what it means to someone is naive. It arrives in the church as the small-group question — “what does this verse mean to you?” — and as the sermon that begins with the text and ends with the preacher. Peter forecloses it: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:20–21). The reasoning is exact. Because the origin of Scripture is not private, its interpretation cannot be private. Joseph said it before Peter did: interpretations belong to God. The interpreter’s task is to find the sense God put there, not to supply one, and the sense is single — the plain, grammatical, historical meaning the Spirit intended, which the Confession makes the rule for settling every controversy.

The mirror error is the priesthood of the specialist: meaning locked away with the scholar, the guru, or the anointed leader who alone can unlock it. Scripture answers both with the perspicuity of the Word and the illumination of the Spirit. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to try even an apostle’s preaching, and were called noble for it. The rule of faith is that Scripture interprets Scripture: the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself, so that when there is a question about the true and full sense of any place, it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. Keep Paul’s discipline too. Where there is no interpreter, silence — because a church may not be occupied with utterance no one can weigh. Edification, not ecstasy, is the measure of everything said in the assembly, and the man who cannot be understood is to speak to himself and to God.
roots_summary: Latin interpres, a go-between; one who bears a meaning across from God’s mind to man’s.
roots_lines: Interpreter — Latin interpres, a broker or agent between parties.
Hebrew melits (H3887), a spokesman or intermediary — Job 33:23; Gen 42:23.
Hebrew pathar (H6622), to interpret a dream — the Joseph narratives (Gen 40–41).
Aramaic peshar — Daniel’s word before Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar.
Greek diermeneutēs (G1328), the required interpreter of a tongue (1Co 14:28).
usage: “Do not interpretations belong to God?” is the charter of the office — and its limit.
Paul forbids uninterpreted tongues in the assembly; edification governs every utterance.
Scripture interprets Scripture: the clearer places settle the sense of the darker.

etymology: From dream, Saxon dream, with the agent ending -er. In Deuteronomy it renders the Hebrew phrase cholem chalom, literally “a dreamer of a dream” — a man who claims revelation received in sleep.
biblical_def: A dreamer, in the biblical sense, is a man who claims that God has spoken to him in sleep. Scripture does not deny that God has so spoken: He warned Abimelech, guided Joseph the husband of Mary, and gave Nebuchadnezzar an empire’s history in a night vision. But Scripture treats the claimant with a settled wariness, and gives Israel the one test that matters. “If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder” — and the sign comes to pass — and he then says, Let us go after other gods, “thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deu 13:1, 3). Mark the order: the wonder is granted and the dreamer is still condemned. Doctrine tries the wonder; the wonder never tries the doctrine. Jeremiah ranks the dreamers with diviners, enchanters, and sorcerers as the voices telling Judah what she wished to hear (Jer 27:9). Joseph’s brothers spit the word as a taunt — “Behold, this dreamer cometh” (Gen 37:19) — and God vindicated him, but by fulfilment across twenty years, not by the dream’s own authority. Jude’s “filthy dreamers” defile the flesh and despise dominion (Jud 1:8): the false dreamer’s life betrays him.
webster_summary: One who dreams; one who claims revelation by dreams; hence an idle visionary, and in Scripture a class of false prophet to be tried by doctrine.
webster_full: DREAMER, n. One who dreams; one that is given to dreams.
One who claims to receive revelation in sleep; “a dreamer of dreams” (Deu 13:1).
An idle or fanciful man; a visionary; one who forms wild schemes and calls them certainties.
In Scripture ranked with diviners, enchanters, and sorcerers among the false voices (Jer 27:9).
Used in scorn of Joseph by his brethren (Gen 37:19), and by Jude of the ungodly who defile the flesh (Jud 1:8).
scriptures: Deu 13:1
If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder,
Deu 13:3

Thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul.
And they said one to another, Behold, this dreamer cometh.
Jer 27:9

Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon:
corruption_summary: The New Apostolic Reformation, Bethel, and IHOP have rebuilt the office of the dreamer of dreams — dreams, visions, and “prophetic words” carried as fresh revelation alongside a canon Scripture declares closed.
corruption_paragraphs: Name it plainly. The New Apostolic Reformation, with Bethel Church in Redding and the International House of Prayer in Kansas City and the wider self-styled apostolic networks, has restored the dreamer of dreams to a standing office. Dreams are logged and published, “words” are delivered over individuals and nations, dream-interpretation is taught as a school subject, and the authority of these utterances is defended by the wonders and healings claimed to attend them. Deu 13:1–3 dismantles the whole apparatus in three verses. God there concedes the sign and the wonder — grants that it may even come to pass — and still commands His people not to hearken, because the message ran contrary to what He had already revealed. The wonder was itself the proving. Doctrine judges the dreamer; the dreamer never judges the doctrine. Add the second test: a prophet whose word fails is not a fallible prophet in training but a false one (Deu 18:20–22), which is the plain answer to the modern excuse that “prophecy today comes at a lower level of accuracy.” Scripture knows no such office.

Behind the practice lies the deeper error — a canon treated as open. The faith was once delivered unto the saints (Jud 1:3); God who spoke in time past by the prophets hath in these last days spoken unto us by His Son (Heb 1:1–2), and the Son’s apostles laid the foundation once (Eph 2:20). A foundation is not laid twice. That is the cessationist position of the Reformed churches, and it is not a diminishment of the Spirit but the honouring of His finished testimony: the Confession says expressly that former ways of God’s revealing His will are now ceased. Recover the sober use of the ordinary means. God still governs sleep and still providentially impresses His people, but no impression carries authority, none binds another man’s conscience, and every one of them stands or falls before the written Word. Try the spirits (1Jn 4:1). The Bereans searched the Scriptures, and were called noble for testing an apostle.
roots_summary: Hebrew cholem chalom, “a dreamer of a dream” — a claimant of revelation, tried by doctrine, not by wonders.
roots_lines: Dreamer — from Saxon dream + -er, one given to dreams.
Hebrew chalam (H2492), to dream; chalom (H2472), a dream.
Deu 13:1 reads literally “a dreamer of a dream” — the claimant, not merely the sleeper.
Listed with diviners, enchanters, and sorcerers in Jer 27:9.
Greek enupniazō in Jud 1:8, of the ungodly who defile the flesh.
usage: Deu 13 grants the wonder and still condemns the dreamer — doctrine tries the sign.
Joseph was vindicated by twenty years of providence, not by the authority of his dream.
No impression, dream, or “word” binds the conscience; the written Word alone does that.

etymology: From the Latin subtilis, finely woven — sub, under, and tela, a web; hence thinness, fineness, and thence craft. The AV spelling keeps the Latin b; the Hebrew is 'ormah, which may be prudence or cunning according to the heart that wields it.
biblical_def: Subtilty is fineness of mind, and Scripture shows it running both ways. In Proverbs it is a good thing sought for the simple: wisdom is written “to give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion” (Pro 1:4) — the shrewdness that keeps a young man from being taken. But the word’s first appearance in the Bible fixes its darker use forever: “Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made” (Gen 3:1). The serpent’s subtilty was not force but a question, and the question moved a hair’s breadth off what God had actually said — Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? That is the pattern of every temptation since: not open denial but a fine misquotation. Isaac names the same thing in his own house: “Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing” (Gen 27:35), and Jacob’s craft to seize what God had already promised him cost him twenty years of exile and a lifetime of being deceived in turn. Paul carries the serpent’s subtilty straight into the church: “I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2Co 11:3). Fineness of speech is the enemy’s chosen instrument, and simplicity toward Christ is the guard.
webster_summary: Thinness or fineness; hence acuteness of mind, and most often in Scripture craft, cunning, and artifice in deceiving.
webster_full: SUBTILTY, n. [L. subtilitas, from subtilis, fine, thin; sub and tela, a web.] Thinness; fineness; exility of parts.
Acuteness of intellect; nicety of discernment; refinement of distinction.
Cunning; artifice; craft; the skill of deceiving under a fair appearance.
“The serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field” (Gen 3:1) — the word’s defining use.
In Pro 1:4 the same Hebrew ('ormah) is a virtue: prudence given to the simple.
scriptures: Gen 3:1
Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?
And he said, Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing.
Pro 1:4
To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion.
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
corruption_summary: The serpent’s method — “Yea, hath God said” — is now the standard hermeneutic: not the denial of Scripture but the endless refinement of it until the command dissolves.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern unbelief rarely arrives as denial. It arrives as subtilty, in exactly the serpent’s form: a question that seems reverent, a distinction that seems careful, a re-reading that seems generous. Did God really say the six days were days, that the marriage bed is one man and one woman for life, that the elders are men, that there is no other name given among men whereby we must be saved? The affirming reading of the sexuality texts does not announce that Paul was wrong; it proposes that Paul meant something narrower than the church has always heard. Progressive evangelicalism does not deny hell; it wonders aloud whether the word means what it has been taken to mean. Each move is a hair’s breadth, and each is fatal, because the serpent needed only a hair’s breadth. Eve’s reply is the warning: she added to the command (neither shall ye touch it) and subtracted from the freedom (every tree became merely we may eat), and a mind already handling the Word loosely was ready for the flat contradiction that followed.

Paul names the antidote and it is not sophistication. It is the simplicity that is in Christ (2Co 11:3) — a plain, whole-hearted holding to what He plainly said. That is not anti-intellectualism; Proverbs commands us to seek subtilty, and the Lord Himself charged His disciples to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. The difference is not the fineness of the mind but the loyalty of the heart. Jacob is the standing case study: he had God’s promise of the blessing already, and he seized it by subtilty anyway, and God gave it — and then broke him at Peniel and left him limping the rest of his life. Craft never gains a thing that faith would not have received more surely and without the wound. Where you find yourself reasoning finely toward a conclusion the flesh already wanted, stop; the fineness is the tell.
roots_summary: Latin subtilis, finely woven; Hebrew 'ormah, shrewdness — prudence in the upright, craft in the serpent.
roots_lines: Subtilty — Latin subtilis (sub + tela, a web): fine-spun, thin.
Hebrew 'ormah (H6195) and the adjective 'arum (H6175) — shrewd, crafty, prudent.
Gen 3:1 and Pro 1:4 use the same root with opposite verdicts: the heart decides.
Greek panourgia (G3834) in 2Co 11:3, all-workingness — the will to do anything to win.
Kin to subtle; the AV spelling preserves the Latin b.
usage: The serpent’s subtilty was a question, not a contradiction — that is still the method.
Proverbs commands subtilty to the simple: shrewdness is a duty, craft is a sin.
Jacob got by subtilty what God had already promised, and limped for it ever after.

etymology: From craft, Saxon cræft, strength, skill, or art, with -iness; the honest sense of skill in a trade decayed into the sense of skill in deceiving. It renders the Hebrew 'ormah and the Greek panourgia, a willingness to do anything whatever to gain the end.
biblical_def: Craftiness is skill turned against the truth — ability used to gain by stratagem what could not be gained honestly. Its great text is Eliphaz’s, and it is one of the few sayings of Job’s friends the New Testament ratifies: “He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong” (Job 5:13). Paul quotes it to the Corinthians, who were dazzled by clever men, and sets it against the whole scheme of worldly cleverness: “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness” (1Co 3:19). The point is not that God outwits the crafty from outside but that He takes them in their craftiness — the net they wove is the net that holds them, and their own counsel carries them headlong. The Gospels show it attempted upon Christ Himself: the spies sent to entangle Him in His words framed the tribute question so that either answer would destroy Him, “but he perceived their craftiness” (Luk 20:23). No man ever took Him in a word. And Paul disavows the thing utterly as a method of ministry: he has renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, “not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth” (2Co 4:2). Open truth, openly stated, is the appointed instrument.
webster_summary: Cunning; artfulness; skill or dexterity employed in deceiving, as distinguished from honest wisdom.
webster_full: CRAFTINESS, n. Cunning; artfulness; stratagem; dexterity in devising and effecting what is intended to deceive.
From craft, Sax. cræft, strength, art, skill — the honest sense retained in handicraft.
“He taketh the wise in their own craftiness” (Job 5:13), quoted by Paul in 1Co 3:19.
Greek panourgia, readiness to do anything; used of the spies who tempted Christ (Luk 20:23).
Renounced by the apostle as a method of ministry (2Co 4:2), and named as the tool of false teachers (Eph 4:14).
scriptures: Job 5:13
He taketh the wise in their own craftiness: and the counsel of the froward is carried headlong.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
But he perceived their craftiness, and said unto them, Why tempt ye me?

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: Craftiness is baptized as strategy in the church — managed messaging, bait-and-switch evangelism, and manipulative appeals — against Paul’s renunciation of every method but the open manifestation of the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: The pragmatic movement in evangelicalism made technique the engine of ministry, and technique easily becomes craftiness. The gospel is withheld until the visitor is emotionally committed; the sermon is engineered around felt needs and the hard doctrines are held back until the hearer is “ready”; the appeal is staged with music and repeated invitation until the will breaks; the church markets itself with the language of the trade show and calls the result the work of the Spirit. Nothing in it is a lie outright, and that is exactly the definition of craftiness — skill employed to secure by stratagem what open truth might not secure. Paul’s renunciation could not be more direct: not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully, but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God (2Co 4:2). His confidence lay in the naked Word addressed to the conscience under God’s eye, and he expressly refused the enticing words of man’s wisdom lest the faith of his hearers should stand in it rather than in the power of God.

The same craftiness works the other side of the pulpit, in the false teachers who carry the immature about with every wind of doctrine “by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive” (Eph 4:14) — a phrase drawn from loaded dice and from an ambush. The remedy Paul gives there is not suspicion but maturity: speaking the truth in love, growing up into Christ, until a congregation is no longer moveable by whoever is most persuasive this year. Recover the promise in Eliphaz’s line, for it is a comfort as well as a warning. God does not merely defeat the crafty; He takes them in the very craft they trusted. Haman hanged on his own gallows; Ahithophel’s counsel was turned to foolishness; the rulers who plotted the cross accomplished the redemption they meant to prevent. Walk in the open. The man with nothing to hide has nothing to be caught in.
roots_summary: Saxon cræft, skill or art, decayed into skill at deceiving; Greek panourgia, willing to do anything.
roots_lines: Craftiness — from Saxon cræft, strength, art, skill (honest sense kept in handicraft).
Hebrew 'ormah (H6195), shrewdness turned to stratagem (Job 5:13).
Greek panourgia (G3834), literally all-workingness — unscrupulous readiness (Luk 20:23; 2Co 4:2).
Job 5:13 is the only saying of Eliphaz quoted approvingly in the New Testament (1Co 3:19).
Eph 4:14 joins it to sleight (Greek kubeia, dice-play) — the rigged game of false teachers.
usage: God takes the wise in their craftiness — the trap they set is the trap that holds them.
Paul renounced craftiness as a method: the open Word to the conscience, or nothing.
Christ perceived the spies’ craftiness; no cleverness ever caught Him in His words.

etymology: From noon — Saxon non, from the Latin nona (hora), the ninth hour of the Roman day, later shifted to midday — joined to day. In Scripture it renders the Hebrew tsohorayim, a dual form meaning “double light,” the hour of the sun’s full strength.
biblical_def: Noonday is the hour of full light, when nothing can hide and nothing needs a lamp; and Scripture uses it as its standard measure of clarity, of vindication, and — by terrible reversal — of judgment. David makes it the promise to the man who commits his way unto the LORD and forbears to fret at the prosperity of the wicked: “he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday” (Psa 37:6). The believer is not told to clear his own name; he is told to wait, because God vindicates at noon. Isaiah gives the same promise to the man who spends himself for the hungry and the afflicted: “then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday” (Isa 58:10) — mercy shown in the dark is repaid with the light of midday. Against these stands the curse. To covenant-breaking Israel Moses says, “thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness” (Deu 28:29): the light is not withdrawn, the eyes are. That is the exact nature of judicial blindness — full noon and a groping man. Job says the same of the crafty (Job 5:14), and the Psalmist names among the terrors from which the LORD covers His own “the destruction that wasteth at noonday” (Psa 91:6), for the enemy strikes in the open as readily as by night.
webster_summary: Midday; the time when the sun is in the meridian; hence the hour of fullest light, used of clarity, vindication, and open assault alike.
webster_full: NOONDAY, n. Midday; twelve o’clock in the day; the time of the sun’s greatest altitude.
adj. Pertaining to midday; meridional; as the noonday heat.
Figuratively, the height or brightest part of anything; perfect clearness.
“He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday” (Psa 37:6).
The hour also of open danger: “the destruction that wasteth at noonday” (Psa 91:6).
scriptures: Psa 37:6
And he shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday.
And if thou draw out thy soul to the hungry, and satisfy the afflicted soul; then shall thy light rise in obscurity, and thy darkness be as the noonday:
And thou shalt grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness, and thou shalt not prosper in thy ways: and thou shalt be only oppressed and spoiled evermore, and no man shall save thee.
Psa 91:6
Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday.
corruption_summary: The promise of Psa 37:6 is claimed as a guarantee of vindication on the believer’s timetable, and the groping of Deu 28:29 is forgotten — that God’s severest judgment leaves the light and darkens the eye.
corruption_paragraphs: The common misuse is impatience dressed as faith. A wronged believer seizes “he shall bring forth thy judgment as the noonday” as a warrant that his name will be cleared, publicly and soon, and treats delay as divine failure — or, worse, takes the vindication into his own hands and calls the campaign an act of trust. But read the whole psalm. The promise is bracketed by commands: fret not, trust in the LORD, delight thyself also in the LORD, commit thy way unto him, rest in the LORD and wait patiently for him. The noonday is God’s hour, not ours, and much of it falls on the other side of the resurrection, when the righteous shall shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Job died without ever hearing the answer given in chapters 38 to 41 explained to him. Christ Himself, reviled, reviled not again, but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously (1Pe 2:23). That is what waiting for noon looks like.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of judicial blindness, which the age has quietly dropped. Deu 28:29 does not say God puts out the sun; it says a man gropes at noonday as the blind gropeth in darkness. The light stands at full strength and the eye cannot use it — which is precisely Paul’s account of the natural man, who holds the truth in unrighteousness, to whom the invisible things of God are clearly seen, so that he is without excuse (Rom 1:18–20), and whose mind the god of this world hath blinded (2Co 4:4). No one perishes for want of light. Isaiah’s answer is the mirror of it: pour yourself out for the hungry and the afflicted, and your own darkness shall be as the noonday. Mercy given in obscurity is repaid with midday, and the God who commanded the light to shine out of darkness shines in the heart to give the light of the knowledge of His glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsohorayim, “double light” — the sun at full strength, the Bible’s measure of clarity and of vindication.
roots_lines: Noonday — noon (Saxon non, from Latin nona hora, the ninth hour) + day.
Hebrew tsohorayim (H6672), a dual form — “double light,” midday.
The Latin nona once marked mid-afternoon; the English noon shifted forward to midday.
Promise: righteousness brought forth as the noonday (Psa 37:6; Isa 58:10).
Curse: groping at noonday, blind in full light (Deu 28:29; Job 5:14).
usage: “Thy judgment as the noonday” is a promise of God’s vindication, on God’s clock.
Groping at noonday is judicial blindness: the light is not taken, the eye is.
Psa 91:6 reminds us the enemy also strikes in broad daylight — noon is no sanctuary of itself.

etymology: From twi-, two or between (as in twice, twain), and light: the between-light, the doubtful glimmer at either end of the day. It renders the Hebrew nesheph, which serves for both the dusk and the dawn — the hour when the eye can no longer tell.
biblical_def: Twilight is the doubtful light at the edges of the day, and Scripture almost always sets a man moving in it. It is first the hour of the sinner who wants a witness and cannot bear one: “The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight, saying, No eye shall see me: and disguiseth his face” (Job 24:15). He does not choose the black of midnight, which would be suspicious, but the half-light, where a face is a smudge; and Job’s indictment is that the man reckons on an eye that cannot see, having forgotten the eye that never closes. Solomon sets the young man void of understanding in the same hour, going toward the strange woman’s corner “in the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night” (Pro 7:9) — and note that the twilight slides into blackness before the paragraph ends, which is how sin always keeps its appointments. But twilight is also the hour of God’s deliverances. The four lepers rose in the twilight to go to the camp of the Syrians and found it empty (2Ki 7:5), because the LORD had made the host to hear a noise of chariots and they “fled in the twilight” (2Ki 7:7), leaving their tents and their horses and their food to feed a starving city. Ezekiel is commanded to dig through the wall and carry out his stuff in the twilight as a sign to a house that would not see (Eze 12:6).
webster_summary: The faint light before sunrise and after sunset; hence any dubious or uncertain half-light, in which the eye cannot rightly judge.
webster_full: TWILIGHT, n. [twi, two or between, and light.] The faint light which is reflected before sunrise and after sunset; the light of the dusk and of the dawn.
Dubious or uncertain view; faint and doubtful knowledge; as the twilight of the understanding.
adj. Obscure; imperfectly illuminated; seen dimly.
The hour of the adulterer’s disguise (Job 24:15) and of the young man’s ruin (Pro 7:9).
Also the hour of the Syrians’ flight and Samaria’s deliverance (2Ki 7:5, 7).
scriptures: The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the twilight, saying, No eye shall see me: and disguiseth his face.
And they rose up in the twilight, to go unto the camp of the Syrians: and when they were come to the uttermost part of the camp of Syria, behold, there was no man there.
Wherefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, and their horses, and their asses, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life.
Eze 12:6

In their sight shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulders, and carry it forth in the twilight: thou shalt cover thy face, that thou see not the ground: for I have set thee for a sign unto the house of Israel.
corruption_summary: The half-light is treated as a place where God does not look — the private hour, the anonymous screen, the sin no one can name — against Scripture’s testimony that the darkness and the light are both alike to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Job’s adulterer has multiplied beyond counting, and the twilight he waits for is now electric. The half-light is the private browser, the deleted thread, the second account, the hotel in another city, the disguised face of an anonymous handle — every arrangement built on the calculation Job puts in the man’s own mouth: No eye shall see me. The calculation is false at the root, and Scripture answers it without pity or exaggeration: the eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the evil and the good; the darkness hideth not from Him, but the night shineth as the day, the darkness and the light are both alike to Him (Psa 139:12); and there is no creature that is not manifest in His sight, all things being naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do (Heb 4:13). The twilight sinner is not hidden. He is merely unobserved by men for a season, which is not the same thing, and God has appointed a day when the hidden things of darkness shall be brought to light and the counsels of the hearts made manifest.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that twilight is God’s hour too, and that He works most often exactly where men can see least. The four lepers rose in the twilight with nothing but the logic of desperation — if we sit still here, we die — and walked into an abandoned camp, because the LORD had already emptied it with a noise no human army made. Samaria was fed that night, and the sneering lord who said it could not be done saw it with his eyes and did not eat thereof. Ezekiel carried his stuff out in the twilight as a sign to a rebellious house. The doubtful light is where faith actually walks: not in noonday certainty but in the half-light, on the word of God alone, one step at a time. Children of the day do not lurk in the dusk to sin; they cross it to obey.
roots_summary: Twi- (between) + light: the between-light; Hebrew nesheph, serving for both dusk and dawn.
roots_lines: Twilight — twi-, two or between (cf. twain, twice) + light.
Hebrew nesheph (H5399) — used of both the evening dusk and the morning glimmer.
Job 24:15 and Pro 7:9 give the sinner’s twilight; 2Ki 7:5, 7 give the LORD’s.
Pro 7:9 stacks the hours — twilight, evening, black and dark night — the slide of sin.
Eze 12:6 makes the twilight removal a prophetic sign to a blind house.
usage: The adulterer chooses twilight, not midnight — enough light to move, too little to be known.
“No eye shall see me” is the twilight creed, and Psa 139:12 is its answer.
The lepers rose in the twilight and found the camp empty: God works in the half-light too.
